### C.4. Full Ablation Results

The expanded results use the same five variants as
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for Large Language Models").
*w/o Atomic Extraction* assigns one role to the complete feedback turn.
*w/o Task Context for Roles* removes $`x_{i}`$ from role assignment.
*w/o Separate Pathways* sends both Fix and Spec through the Generalist
while continuing to exclude Null. *w/o Specialist* discards Spec
supervision, and *w/o KEEP Supervision* trains the Specialist only on
APPLY targets.

The two-backbone results match the main ablation trends. Removing the
task context from role assignment produces the largest MemoryBench
average and AlpacaEval 2.0 losses on both backbones. Sending Fix and
Spec through one Generalist or discarding Spec both underperform the
complete model. Removing KEEP supervision produces the largest IFEval
loss on both backbones.

### C.6. Feedback Processing and Specialist-Target Audit

##### Extraction and role assignment.

The extractor observes $`(x_{i},y_{i}^{\mathrm{log}},u_{i})`$ and
returns an ordered list of minimal components, possibly empty. Role
assignment is a separate call that observes only $`(x_{i},c_{ij})`$. It
assigns Fix when every fully valid response to $`x_{i}`$ must satisfy
the component, Spec when the component is task-compatible but omissible,
and Null when no reliable positive update is supported.

The extraction audit samples 300 processed root tasks per source, split
evenly across the Qwen3-8B and Ministral3-14B processing pipelines. The
independent judge receives the logged interaction and extracted list,
but not component roles or downstream results, and checks coverage,
faithfulness, and atomicity. The role audit samples 500 components from
each assigned role and source, split evenly across the two processing
backbones. The judge receives only $`(x_{i},c_{ij})`$ and independently
assigns a Fix-like, Spec-like, Null-like, or uncertain label.

| Source      | $`n`$ | Coverage | Faithful | Atomic | All  |

| WildFB      | 300   | 89.0     | 95.3     | 90.0   | 84.0 |

##### Specialist targets.

For each source, we sample 250 target-KEEP and 250 target-APPLY states,
split evenly across the two backbone pipelines. The judge receives
$`(x_{i},y_{i}^{G},C_{i}^{S})`$ but not the constructed target. It
independently determines whether the current task–response state
supports a missing compatible refinement and therefore calls for KEEP or
APPLY. For APPLY states, a separate pass checks whether the guidance is
grounded in $`C_{i}^{S}`$, covers the missing compatible changes, and
remains residual rather than replacing the response. This audit
evaluates the offline targets rather than the trained Specialist itself.

The analysis manifest contains 845 MemoryBench and 14,094 WildFB root
tasks. Complete outputs are available for 834 and 13,866 tasks,
respectively; incomplete provider output is the only exclusion. The
standardized comparison uses seven shared task-operation by
verifiability strata, covering 790 MemoryBench and 5,599 WildFB root
tasks. The standardized results therefore describe the shared-support
task distribution rather than the full WildFB training distribution.
These details yield the values reported in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5. Analysis ‣ Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for Large Language Models").

### C.8. Stage-wise Contributions

Subtracting adjacent endpoints reproduces all $`\Delta_{\mathrm{G}}`$
and $`\Delta_{\mathrm{S}}`$ values in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2. Stage-wise Contributions ‣ 5. Analysis ‣ Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for Large Language Models").
The corresponding decision counts also recover the reported APPLY and
edit rates. Edited never exceeds APPLY; MMLU-Pro is the all-KEEP case
and shows no Specialist increment.
